templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Cause/effect: need or judgment, then the action it motivates
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: Chilean poet Nicanor Parra called his writing “antipoetry.” Critics have generally read it as a rejection of the lyric tradition, with its elevated diction and solemn emotion. ______ Parra’s antipoems keep many of that tradition’s outward conventions, such as line breaks and stanzas, but he fills those familiar forms with clichés, everyday speech, and deadpan humor that deflates any grandeur.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences say that critics see Parra’s antipoetry as a rejection of the lyric tradition. The blank sentence first admits a point that seems to cut against that claim: the antipoems still use line breaks and stanzas. Then, after “but,” it returns to the main claim by showing how Parra fills those forms with clichés and jokes. “Of course” signals this kind of concession before a turn.

A.why_wrong: Critics’ reading of antipoetry as a rejection of tradition does not cause Parra’s poems to keep line breaks and stanzas.

B.why_wrong: Keeping the tradition’s outward conventions is not like rejecting that tradition; it is a point that seems to cut against it.

C.why_wrong: “Moreover” would add a further point in support of the claim, but the poems’ use of line breaks and stanzas is a concession, which the clause after “but” then answers.

items.notes: Plan band_target 7, but spec/rw/band7/transitions.md has no band-7 K1 official item and says not to push K1 to band 7; written as a strong band 6 (band_target 6). items.passage: Wildfires in the United States are often imagined as natural disasters, sparked when lightning strikes parched vegetation. Yet when researchers examined government records of more than 1.5 million wildfires that burned between 1992 and 2012, they found that lightning had caused only about one in six. ______ the fires were started by people, through campfires, debris burning, equipment sparks, and arson.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives the common picture: wildfires start when lightning strikes. The second says that in the records, lightning started only about one in six fires. The blank sentence names what happened in most of the other cases: people started the fires. “More often” signals that this cause was more common than the lightning the first sentence describes.

A.why_wrong: That people started most of the fires is not true in spite of the finding about lightning; it is what the finding implies about the rest of the fires.

C.why_wrong: The small share of lightning fires did not cause people to start the others; the clause reports the more common cause, not a result.

D.why_wrong: The clause does not add a separate finding; it tells what caused most of the fires that lightning did not, completing the comparison with the lightning picture.

More often'), not of the band-7 d3b7d7a3, where the student infers the frequency from 'complicates this popular narrative' behind a semicolon and interrupter; here the key is read off the number and every decoy dies on the same fact. items.passage: The 2019 miniseries Chernobyl dramatizes the 1986 explosion at a Soviet nuclear power plant, following the scientists and officials who struggled to contain the radiation. ______ Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir built the show’s eerie, pulsing score largely from hums, clanks, and drones that she recorded inside a nuclear plant in Lithuania that had been shut down.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says the series is about the explosion at a nuclear power plant. The blank sentence says that its music was made from sounds recorded inside a nuclear power plant. Music drawn from such a place suits a story about a nuclear disaster, so “Fittingly” is the logical choice.

B.why_wrong: The way the score was made does not contrast with the subject of the series; it matches it.

C.why_wrong: The first sentence is not something the score was made in spite of or without regard to; the score’s source matches the series’ subject.

D.why_wrong: The sentence about the score does not reword the description of what the series dramatizes.

items.passage: Railway engineers in British India generally constructed principal lines to a broad gauge. Spacing the rails about 1.7 meters apart stabilized heavy trains traveling at speed across the plains. ______ the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, opened in 1881, was built with rails 0.6 meters apart, a gauge selected to let its locomotives negotiate the hairpin curves and switchbacks of a mountain ascent.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe the usual practice: main lines in British India were built to a broad gauge. The blank sentence describes an exception: the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway was built with rails much closer together, for the sake of its mountain route. “Nevertheless” signals that this railway departed from the usual practice.

A.why_wrong: The broad gauge of the main lines, chosen for heavy trains on the plains, did not cause the Darjeeling line to be built narrow; the narrow gauge was chosen for the mountains.

B.why_wrong: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway is not an instance of a line laid to a broad gauge; it is an exception to that practice.

D.why_wrong: The Darjeeling line does not add another point about broad-gauge lines; it departs from that practice.

items.notes: Band-7 gate (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 6): key outside the core 13, no sequence or summary decoy; register 5.22 chars per word, held near CB per the 2026-10-16 register rule rather than the 5.3 gate. Band-7 moves (C3 recipe, fc95a352): a habit, then a one-off exception keyed with “Nevertheless”, no other adversative option, and the exception given a purpose; an instance trap (a named railway right after a statement about railways) beside the model’s cause and additive decoys. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

fixes: hardened: dropped 'only' before '0.6 meters apart', so the student must compare the two gauges (1.7 against 0.6) instead of reading a contrast cue, which strengthens the For example instance trap without adding ambiguity
review.notes: No fact check (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation; all named people are real and researchers behind findings are left unnamed. Second-sense check: Nevertheless is the only adversative; For example fails because the 0.6 m gauge is not broad.

band7.why: Mirrors fc95a352 move for move: a habit (broad gauge for principal lines), a one-off exception given a purpose (hairpin curves), Nevertheless in its exception role with no other adversative option, CB's cause and additive decoys. After dropping 'only', the contrast rests on comparing 1.7 and 0.6, and a first-read misreading (a named railway in British India right after a statement about how its lines were built) pulls a strong student to For example. Fails the spec's automatic proxy 3 (adversative key) and register gate 4 (about 5.2), as fc95a352 itself does on proxy 3.

items.passage: The coco de mer, a palm restricted to two islands in the Seychelles, produces the heaviest seeds in the plant kingdom, sometimes exceeding 10 kilograms. ______ certain orchids produce microscopic seeds weighing approximately a millionth of a gram, light enough to disperse on air currents like dust particles.

items.explanation: The first sentence says the coco de mer produces the heaviest seeds of any plant. The blank sentence gives the weight of orchid seeds, which are almost weightless. “By comparison” signals this contrast between two numbers for the same attribute.

B.why_wrong: Orchid seeds are not like the coco de mer seed; they are at the opposite extreme of weight.

C.why_wrong: Orchid seeds are not an example of the heavy seeds of the coco de mer; they are at the opposite extreme.

items.passage: Most fish are ectotherms: their body temperature fluctuates with that of the surrounding water. items.explanation: The first sentence says that most fish have the same temperature as the water around them. The blank sentence says the opah keeps its body warmer than the water. “In contrast” signals that the opah differs from most fish in this way.

A.why_wrong: The opah is a fish, but it is an exception to the pattern described for most fish, not an instance of it.

B.why_wrong: Other fish matching the water’s temperature does not cause the opah to stay warmer than the water.

C.why_wrong: The opah does not do what most fish do; it does the opposite.

items.passage: In 1991, Japanese researchers collected tiny eel larvae west of the Mariana Islands, evidence that the Japanese eel spawns somewhere nearby. In 2008, scientists captured mature adults along an undersea ridge in that region. ______ in 2009, researchers retrieved freshly spawned eggs there, the first ever recovered in the wild.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage lists, in order of date, steps in the search for the place where the Japanese eel spawns: larvae in 1991, adults ready to spawn in 2008, and then eggs in 2009, the most direct evidence of all. “Finally” signals that the 2009 discovery came last and completed the search.

A.why_wrong: The 2009 discovery of eggs is not an example of the 2008 capture of adult eels; it is the next and last step.

B.why_wrong: Collecting eggs in 2009 is a new event, not a rewording of catching adult eels in 2008.

D.why_wrong: The earlier finds are not irrelevant to the 2009 discovery; they led the search to the place where the eggs were found.

items.passage: Icelandic has changed so little across the centuries that modern speakers can read medieval sagas with relative ease. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe a concern: English words might disrupt a language that has changed little in centuries. The blank sentence describes the action taken because of it: specialists create Icelandic names for new things instead of borrowing English ones. “Accordingly” signals an action that follows from the concern.

A.why_wrong: Coining Icelandic words does not contrast with the concern about English words; it is a response to that concern.

C.why_wrong: The committees’ practice does not spell out the planners’ worry in more exact terms; it is an action the worry leads to.

items.passage: Western saws cut on the push stroke, so their steel blades must be thick and rigid enough to resist bending as the woodworker drives them forward. Japanese saws, ______ cut on the pull stroke, which keeps the blade under tension and allows it to be considerably thinner.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says Western saws cut when pushed and need thick blades. The blank sentence says Japanese saws cut when pulled and can have thin blades. “In contrast” signals this difference between the two kinds of saws.

A.why_wrong: Japanese saws are not an example of saws that cut on the push stroke; they work the opposite way.

C.why_wrong: The design of Western saws does not cause Japanese saws to cut on the pull stroke.

D.why_wrong: Japanese saws do not work like Western saws; they cut in the opposite direction.

items.passage: After taking power in 1868, Japan’s Meiji government set out to build railways, factories, and schools modeled on those of Europe and the United States. However, the country had few engineers or teachers trained in Western methods. ______ the government hired thousands of foreign specialists, known as oyatoi gaikokujin, to direct projects and train Japanese students.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe a need: Japan wanted Western-style railways, factories, and schools but lacked people trained to build and run them. The blank sentence describes the action the government took to meet that need. “For this reason” signals that the hiring was done because of the shortage.

B.why_wrong: Hiring foreign experts is not like the shortage of trained workers; it is a response to it.

C.why_wrong: Hiring foreign experts is not an example of the shortage of trained workers; it is what the government did about it.

D.why_wrong: The passage is not listing points in order; the hiring follows from the shortage described before it.

items.passage: Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx wanted his gardens to celebrate Brazil’s own plants rather than imitate the formal European gardens then fashionable in Rio de Janeiro. ______ he made dozens of trips into Brazil’s forests and mountains to collect native plants, several of them previously unknown to science.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence states Burle Marx’s goal: gardens that celebrate Brazil’s own plants. The blank sentence describes what he did to reach that goal: he traveled to collect native plants. “With this in mind” signals an action taken because of that goal.

A.why_wrong: Collecting native plants does not contrast with his wish to celebrate Brazil’s plants; it serves that wish.

B.why_wrong: His trips are not similar to his goal; they are the means he used to reach it.

C.why_wrong: The trips do not restate Burle Marx’s wish in more exact terms; they are an action he took because of it.
